themes.name: Incentives, Not Architecture
themes.plain: Many of these problems are fights over money and credit, not engineering gaps. Teams and outside partners each gain from keeping their own number or their own channel goal, so no schema, protocol, or dashboard can settle the argument for them.
themes.evidence: On cross-channel journey orchestration all three models land on incentives: no neutral party can price a customer's attention, the objective is ungovernable while incentives are split, and channel owners must accept that sending nothing is sometimes best; the semantic context layer answers say teams define terms differently on purpose, and the downstream consent answers say ad platforms are rewarded for staying opaque.

themes.name: Start From What Already Failed
themes.plain: Every model opens by digging into what the company already did: rejected content, past disputes, real logs, one live use case. Nobody starts by designing the ideal system on paper.
themes.evidence: First moves include instrumenting one honest cross-channel contact ledger and unifying exposure logging for a single journey, pulling the last 200 rejected content pieces and auditing legal rejections, reading the actual SQL behind every definition of customer, rebuilding data exits from network and vendor logs, and measuring what share of interactions carry a verified login.

themes.name: Chokepoint Before Trust
themes.plain: When the models cannot trust who is acting or where data goes, they build one door they own and force everything through it. Gateway, log, cap, expire, because a sent message or a spent budget cannot be taken back.
themes.evidence: On safe agent execution all three route writes through a proxy or gateway with kill switches and hard limits on budget and audience size; on downstream consent one model replaces perpetual audience lists with short-lived cohorts that expire; on journey orchestration one model proposes a single absolute contact limit across all channels.

themes.name: Nobody Can Verify Downstream
themes.plain: Once data or an instruction leaves your own systems, you cannot see inside the partner, ad platform, or trained model that received it. So compliance and safety can only be estimated from outside, never proven.
themes.evidence: The downstream consent answers all say the same thing: you cannot inspect an ad platform audience, an agency segment, or a trained model, so deletion and suppression can only be inferred; the safe agent execution answers add that vendor APIs offer no rollback for irreversible effects.

themes.name: Agents Break Web Assumptions
themes.plain: Software agents now browse, buy, and act for people, but the systems underneath were built for humans clicking pages. The stack cannot tell who is on the other end, what they are allowed to do, or what a term in their request even means.
themes.evidence: The agentic traffic answers say any signal an agent volunteers is worthless unless the operator has something to lose, and agents will pose as human when human interfaces get better prices; the safe agent execution and semantic context layer answers add that platforms lack agent identity, rollback, and machine-readable definitions.
